title: The late hare
hookLine: the smallest animal walks to the lion slowly, on purpose (Masnavi 1)

lines: THE LOT FALLS ON THE HARE.
cards: Have you ever been late on purpose? You let the pasta water boil a little longer so the argument in the kitchen could cool. You walked around the block before the meeting, so you'd walk in calm instead of furious.
Something says hurry. But sometimes slowing down is exactly the right move. The animals have made their deal with the lion: one of them every day, chosen by lot.
The days go by. Then the lot falls on a hare, small and easy to overlook. Today, the late hare.

teach.h: GIVE ME TIME: I HAVE A PLAN.
teach.b: The hare doesn't run and hide. He tells the other animals: give me a little time. I have a plan.
They're outraged. Who do you think you are? We've kept our promise to the lion all this time, and you'll ruin it.
You, a hare, cleverer than all of us? The hare answers calmly: God gives understanding to the weak as well as the strong.
Rumi, through him, points to the bee: a tiny creature, and yet, the Quran says, God inspired it to build and make honey. Size isn't wisdom. So they let him go.
And he walks. Slowly. He stops.
He thinks. He lingers. Meanwhile the lion waits, hour after hour, no meal.
He paces, roars, claws the ground. I knew it, he says to himself. They cheated me.
Rumi spends lines on that rage: how anger blinds, and how being sure of yourself can make you easy to fool.
By the time the hare finally strolls up, the lion is almost out of his mind. Why are you late? he roars. The hare bows and begins a story, which comes tomorrow.
For today, notice the strategy. The hare can't outfight the lion, and he can't outrun him forever. But he can choose his pace, and the lion can't.
He slows down on purpose, and the lion's own hurry becomes his weakness.

how: The lion and the hare is a Masnavi story with older roots in the animal fables of Kalila and Dimna, which descend from the Indian Panchatantra; Rumi retells it with his own long reflections.

games.why: the hare takes his time on the road. he can't outfight the lion, but he can choose his pace, and the lion can't.

practice: Take the next thing you do, standing up, reaching for your phone, even the next breath, and do it at half speed. Notice the urge to hurry; let it be there, and don't obey it.
Breathe out slower than you'd like, and feel what it's like to set your own pace.
